neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place; knows month and year but states the date as three days prior. MMSE 21/30, losing points on recall (0/3 at 5 minutes), orientation (2 points lost), attention/serial sevens (3 errors), and copy of intersecting pentagons (incomplete). Clock drawing test shows all numbers present but bunched to the right side of the clock face, with hands set to an incorrect time. Unable to recall any of the 3 registered words after 5 minutes, even with phonemic cues. Naming intact for common objects but unable to name the stem of a watch or the eraser on a pencil. Repetition intact. Follows two-step commands but has difficulty with three-step commands. Judgment mildly impaired on hypothetical scenarios.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements full bilaterally without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact. Face symmetric with normal strength. Hearing mildly diminished bilaterally, age-appropriate. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone in all extremities. No rigidity. Strength 5/5 throughout. No pronator drift. No tremor, chorea, or myoclonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch and pinprick in all extremities. Vibration mildly diminished at bilateral great toes, otherwise intact. Proprioception intact at the toes bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles tendons bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady with normal base and stride. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No festination, no shuffling.
neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No grasp or palmomental reflexes. No snout reflex. No myoclonus.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory problems over two years, getting noticeably worse in the last eight months
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Sharma is a 69-year-old right-handed retired postal worker who is brought to the outpatient neurology clinic by her wife, Dorothy, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties. Dorothy reports that she first noticed something was wrong approximately two years ago when her wife began misplacing her car keys and wallet repeatedly, something she had never done before. She initially attributed it to normal aging, but over the past eight months the problems have become much more apparent and concerning. She now frequently asks the same questions multiple times within a single conversation, sometimes within minutes, and does not seem to recall that she already asked. She has forgotten several scheduled appointments with her primary care physician and her barber despite having kept these routines reliably for decades. Last Thanksgiving, she could not remember the name of her grandson's wife, whom she has known for six years, causing considerable embarrassment and family concern. Her daughter reports that when she calls to tell her about upcoming family plans, she has no recollection of the conversation the following day. She was previously an avid reader of history books but has stopped reading in the past year because she says she cannot remember what happened in previous chapters. She attempted to help her wife with preparing their tax documents this past winter, a task she had always managed independently, but became confused by the forms and gave up after making several errors. Her wife has since taken over managing their finances. She has also had difficulty operating the new television remote control and the microwave, despite being shown how to use them on multiple occasions. She got lost driving home from the hardware store two months ago, a route she has taken hundreds of times over thirty years, and had to call her wife for directions. Since then, the family has asked her not to drive alone. She continues to dress and bathe independently, though her wife notes she has worn the same outfit two days in a row on several occasions without realizing it. She denies any hallucinations, and her wife confirms there have been no episodes of seeing things that are not there. There have been no significant personality or behavioral changes, though she has become somewhat more withdrawn and less interested in socializing with friends from her lodge. She denies headaches, seizures, falls, tremor, or difficulty walking. Her sleep has been unremarkable with no acting out of dreams reported by her wife.

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. The informant history and the loss of instrumental independence establish decline from a previous level and place the syndrome at the dementia rather than the mild threshold. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

findings.test: Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test - Immediate Recall
Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test - Delayed Recall

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a severely amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Episodic memory is profoundly impaired: RAVLT delayed recall below the 1st percentile and immediate recall at the 3rd percentile, consistent with a storage-type encoding deficit that does not benefit from phonemic cuing. Semantic fluency (Category Fluency — Animals, 8th percentile) and confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 18th percentile) are significantly impaired. Both letter fluency (FAS, 22nd percentile) and executive set-shifting (Trail Making B, 12th percentile) are reduced. Visuoconstructive ability (Rey Complex Figure Copy, 20th percentile) is below expected norms. Processing speed (Trail Making A, 25th percentile) is at the lower limit of normal. Screening scores: MMSE 21/30, MoCA 16/30. Mood screening is borderline (GDS 5/15); cognitive deficits are disproportionate to any mood contribution. Profile is consistent with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, multi-domain type

differential.key_features: DLB must be actively excluded by absence of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; biomarkers and (when needed) DaTscan can distinguish if features emerge
FTD typically presents with prominent personality change, disinhibition, or progressive aphasia rather than amnesia; positive amyloid biomarkers further argue against FTLD pathology
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or sleep-related cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Screening labs exclude hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, and HIV; the progressive amnestic profile would not normalize with treatment of any of these alone

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed clinical history from patient and informant, including timeline, cognitive domains affected, functional decline, mood, sleep, and medication review
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradually progressive cognitive change with informant-confirmed functional impairment in IADLs

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and/or MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment on MoCA more sensitive than MMSE; non-focal neurological exam (or variant-specific findings — visuospatial in PCA, language in lvPPA, behavioral in frontal AD)

optimal_actions.action: Order reversible-cause labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, folate; consider RPR/HIV per risk)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) excluded; identify and address co-morbid metabolic factors

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral medial-temporal / hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 2-3) with temporoparietal cortical volume loss

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Amnestic profile with disproportionate impairment of delayed recall and limited benefit from cueing, plus involvement of at least one other cognitive domain

optimal_actions.action: Order CSF biomarkers (Aβ42, Aβ42/40 ratio, p-tau, total tau) for ATN classification
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduced Aβ42 (or reduced Aβ42/40 ratio) with elevated p-tau supporting A+T+ profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order amyloid PET when CSF biomarkers are unavailable or when diagnostic uncertainty persists after clinical assessment and MRI
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive cortical amyloid retention (SUVr above positivity threshold) confirming amyloid pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order FDG-PET to assess regional metabolism and distinguish AD from frontotemporal dementia or other neurodegenerative patterns
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism characteristic of Alzheimer pattern

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No clinically significant interactions; counsel on GI side effects and bradycardia risk

optimal_actions.action: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Impairment documented on a validated instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile and informant-confirmed decline from a previous level, staged by whether independence in instrumental activities is preserved (mild cognitive impairment) or lost (dementia)

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family, discuss prognosis, advance directives, and driving / safety assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and caregiver engaged in care planning; safety concerns (driving, finances, medication management) addressed

useless_tools.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF AT(N) markers or amyloid PET) when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

key_educational_points: Early AD classically presents with progressive episodic memory loss as the predominant symptom
Reversible causes of dementia must be systematically excluded with appropriate laboratory testing
Comorbid vascular disease is common in elderly AD patients and may contribute to cognitive decline (mixed dementia)
APOE E4/E4 homozygosity confers the highest genetic risk for late-onset AD
Hippocampal atrophy on MRI is a supportive but not pathognomonic finding for AD
CSF biomarkers (Abeta42, phospho-tau, total tau) can confirm neurodegenerative pathology in vivo and are increasingly used in clinical practice
Cholinesterase inhibitors remain first-line pharmacotherapy for mild-to-moderate AD
Driving safety must be addressed when patients demonstrate navigational impairment
